locator: Epidemiologic Analysis of Drug Overdose Death Data › Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 3rd paragraph
extracted: As the review reports (citing Hargrove et al., 2018): after routine gabapentin testing was introduced in Kentucky in July 2014, the prevalence of gabapentin among drug overdose decedents rose from 2.9% in 2013 to 17% in 2014, which the review attributes to the new testing; the authors warn that gradual improvements in procedures produce smaller, harder-to-detect shifts.

A false negative was a death with very low or no suspicion at referral in which toxicologic analysis determined a drug toxicity to be the cause of death in the absence of significant findings at autopsy, so the 115 deaths not suspected were identified by toxicology. In the Discussion the authors say their results support a correct determination of drug-related deaths from scene investigation, external examination and comprehensive toxicology in a majority of cases, a few having another cause. They summarize two other US studies (not read here): in one, toxicology detected no substance to explain the death, with another cause concluded, in 11% to 13% of suspected drug deaths; in the other, three pathologists given history, scene, external findings and toxicology, without internal examination findings, determined the correct cause and manner in 75% to 80% of 60 cases selected from 629.

locator: Question 1 (which deaths require jurisdiction and autopsy), 1st and 5th paragraphs (p. 153); References, reference 15 (p. 158)
extracted: The panel cites one study of deaths from drug toxicity (reference 15, Dye et al., 2019) for external examination being less accurate than autopsy even when scene findings strongly suggest overdose, without giving a figure. NAME's standards allow autopsy to be deferred in one subset of suspected overdose deaths, delayed deaths due to overdose or suspected overdose; the panel agrees, provided the medical record from hospital admission to death is reviewed and any admission blood or urine is sought.

The authors summarize that about 83% of offices reported access to toxicology and over 1 in 10 reported none, and note that offices reporting no access may have their cases processed through an autopsy provider or a state medical examiner office, and that some offices serve rural and frontier areas with few or no deaths in a year (about 300 reported five or fewer deaths a year).

(2013) found 85% of poisoning deaths in Maryland and over 40% in Utah classed as undetermined intent against 8% nationally; as of 2016 the share of drug poisoning deaths with undetermined intent still ranged from 1% (Connecticut, Massachusetts) to 68% (Maryland), and the authors suggest that medical examiner and coroner office policies not aligned with professional recommendations may influence this variation; the review does not name the states' system types here.

locator: Background, 4th paragraph; Methods, 6th paragraph; Results, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion, 6th paragraph
extracted: Medical examiners are described as typically appointed physicians and coroners as elected laypeople, with requirements varying by state (several states require coroners to be physicians). The preferred models include state indicators so as to compare county systems within states; Indiana relies exclusively on county coroners and North Carolina has a centralized medical examiner system (Results, 2nd paragraph), as does Maryland (Results, 4th paragraph), so these three states give no within-state contrast (editors' inference). The authors report that the indicators for whether an opioid or alcohol test was recorded were largely not significant.

extracted: Before the switch, two of the seven analysed states had justices of the peace (West Virginia, Arizona), two coroners (New Mexico, New Jersey), and one each a physician coroner (Massachusetts), a locally appointed physician (New Hampshire) and a magistrate coroner (Alaska) (Table 1). The model is a single equation fitted to pooled state-years, with no stated allowance for repeated observations of the same state. Figure 1 shows the pairs moving differently after the switch: New Jersey's non-specific share stayed well above New York's, while New Mexico, West Virginia and Massachusetts lay below their controls and Arizona and Nevada moved together; no state-by-state estimates are reported.

Support for harm reduction was higher after older than younger decedents (F(1,1230) = 4.5, p = .035), printed as 22.98 (SD 5.09) against 23.57 (SD 4.78); no main effect of gender (F = .0, p = .802) or drug (F = .0, p = .922); a profile-plot comparison says support was higher after the older than the younger ecstasy decedent, printed with F(1,1230) = 4.8, p = .029 and means 22.7 against 23.89. Table 1 gives condition means for stigma from 38.6 (Jane, young, ecstasy) to 50.1 (John, old, heroin). Editors' calculation from Table 1 weighted by group size: harm-reduction support older 23.6 against younger 23.0, in the ecstasy stories 23.9 against 22.7 and in the heroin stories 23.3 against 23.3, so the printed means are in reverse order (card reporting issue 1); from the cell means and the pooled SD (4.93), the age-by-drug interaction recomputes at F about 5.4 and the within-ecstasy age difference at about 10, while the same method reproduces the printed age main effect (4.6 against 4.5), so the printed F = 4.8 is most likely the interaction test.
